# Understanding Models and Equations {#sec-lecture-02}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
library(gt)
library(gapminder)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)
```

::: {.callout-note .box-goals title="In this chapter"}
After this chapter, you can:

- draw the model of a set of hypotheses, with the right shapes and arrows
- count the hypotheses that a model tests, main effects and interaction effects
- write the equation of a model and say which estimate $b$ tests which hypothesis
- read the intercept, the estimate and the error on a prediction line
- write a model in the DOT language and an equation in LaTeX

You need nothing but a pen. For the last exercises, a DOT editor such as <http://viz-js.com/> and a LaTeX equation editor such as <https://latex.codecogs.com/eqneditor/editor.php> help.
:::

In research outputs, all the sections are linked (@fig-l02-sections).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-l02-sections
%%| fig-cap: "The sections of a research output are linked."
%%| fig-alt: "Flow chart from left to right with five boxes, Introduction, Literature Review, Methods, Results, and Discussion and Conclusion, each linked to the next by an arrow."
%%| fig-width: 5.7
flowchart LR
  A[Introduction] --> B[Literature<br/>Review]
  B --> C[Methods]
  C --> D[Results]
  D --> E[Discussion &<br/>Conclusion]
```

To understand the statistics in the results section, it is essential to identify the concepts presented in each section: the variables, the hypotheses, the model and equation, and the statistical test (@fig-l02-concepts).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-l02-concepts
%%| fig-cap: "The concepts to identify between the sections of a research output."
%%| fig-alt: "The same flow chart with a label on each arrow: Variables between Introduction and Literature Review, Hypotheses between Literature Review and Methods, Model and Equation between Methods and Results, and Statistical Test between Results and Discussion and Conclusion."
%%| fig-width: 5.7
flowchart LR
  A[Introduction] -- Variables --> B[Literature<br/>Review]
  B -- Hypotheses --> C[Methods]
  C -- Model &<br/>Equation --> D[Results]
  D -- Statistical<br/>Test--> E[Discussion &<br/>Conclusion]
```

The variables and the hypotheses are the subject of @sec-lecture-01. This chapter is about the next two concepts, the model and the equation. @sec-l02-models shows how to represent the model tested in a paper: the rules to follow, the types of model, what makes a good model and the tools to draw one. @sec-l02-equations explains the equation used to test the hypotheses: its coefficients, the role of the intercept and the ways to write an equation. The chapter ends with the steps to follow from the variables to the equation (@sec-l02-conclusion).

@fig-l02-roadmap shows these steps as one path. Each step builds on the one before it, and the test of the estimates is the subject of @sec-lecture-04.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-roadmap
#| fig-cap: "From the variables to the test: the steps of this chapter and of the next ones."
#| fig-alt: "Five boxes in a row joined by arrows. Variables: role and type. Hypotheses: Ha and H0. Model: one arrow per hypothesis. Equation: one b per arrow. Test: of each b, Chapter 4."
#| fig-height: 1.4
roadmap <- tribble(
  ~step,        ~detail,
  "Variables",  "role and type",
  "Hypotheses", "Ha and H0",
  "Model",      "one arrow\nper hypothesis",
  "Equation",   "one b\nper arrow",
  "Test",       "of each b\n(Chapter 4)"
)

flow_chart(roadmap)
```

## Model representation in the method section of an academic research paper {#sec-l02-models}

### The method section {#sec-l02-method}

The method section of an academic paper is always structured in the same way:

1. **Observations.** A short section presenting where the data are coming from. If they are coming from human participants, then their average age and gender are indicated.
2. **Variables.** A short section presenting each variable as well as their type and role.
3. **Procedure.** A short section presenting how the data were collected.
4. **Data analytics.** A short section to display how the hypotheses are tested, by displaying a graphical representation of the model and its corresponding equation(s).

The last part, the model and its equation, is the topic of this chapter.

### Rules and notation {#sec-l02-rules}

A **model** is an overview of the predicted relationships between the variables stated in the hypotheses. To represent a model, you must follow four rules:

- **Rule 1**: all the arrows correspond to a hypothesis to be tested.
- **Rule 2**: all the tested hypotheses have to be represented with an arrow.
- **Rule 3**: hypotheses using the same outcome variable should be included in the same model.
- **Rule 4**: only one outcome variable is included in each model (except for SEM models, see @sec-l02-sem).

The arrows have a meaning. A simple arrow is a **main effect** and a crossing arrow is an **interaction effect** (@fig-l02-arrows). By default, an interaction effect involves the test of the main effect hypotheses of all the predictors involved.

::: {#fig-l02-arrows}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-arrows-main
//| fig-cap: "A simple arrow is a main effect."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.11
//| fig-height: 0.52

digraph {
  rankdir="LR"
  node [shape=box]
  Predictor -> Outcome
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-arrows-interaction
//| fig-cap: "A crossing arrow is an interaction effect."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 and a box labelled Outcome joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Outcome. A box labelled Predictor 2 has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.58
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

The two kinds of arrows of a model.
:::

The shapes also have a meaning. **Squares** are actual **measures** or **items**, whereas **circles** are **latent variables** related to measures or items. For example, $Salary$ is directly measured (in \$, € or £) so it is a square, whereas $Job\,Satisfaction$ is a latent variable with several questions so it is a circle. Items used for latent variables can be omitted in a model, because the variables are the most important.

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: latent variable"}
A **latent variable** is a variable that is not measured directly but through several measures or items, such as the questions of a job satisfaction scale. In a model, a latent variable is drawn as a circle (or an oval) and a measure or item as a square.
:::

### Main effects and interaction effects {#sec-l02-effects}

The relationship between one predictor and one outcome variable is represented by a simple arrow (@fig-l02-main). The first model tests one main effect hypothesis. The second model, with two predictors and one outcome variable, tests two main effect hypotheses.

::: {#fig-l02-main}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-main-one
//| fig-cap: "One predictor and one outcome variable."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.23
//| fig-height: 0.52

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-main-two
//| fig-cap: "Two predictors and one outcome variable."
//| fig-alt: "Two boxes, Predictor 1 and Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.23
//| fig-height: 1.16

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

Models with main effects only.
:::

An **interaction** (also called **moderation**) means that the effect of Predictor 1 on the outcome variable will be different according to the possibilities of Predictor 2. It is represented by the crossing arrow in @fig-l02-interaction, which gives exactly the same results as the model where the interaction is a predictor of its own. This model tests three hypotheses: 2 main effects and 1 interaction effect.

::: {#fig-l02-interaction}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-interaction-effects
//| fig-cap: "Effects representation."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 and a box labelled Outcome joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Outcome. A box labelled Predictor 2 has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.58
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-interaction-term
//| fig-cap: "Exactly the same results, with the interaction as a predictor of its own."
//| fig-alt: "Three boxes, Predictor 1, Predictor 2 and Predictor 1 X Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 3.16
//| fig-height: 1.79

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 1 X Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

Two equivalent representations of an interaction effect.
:::

What does an interaction look like in the data? @fig-l02-interaction-lines draws the effect of Predictor 1 on the outcome for the two categories of Predictor 2. Without an interaction, the effect of Predictor 1 is the same in both categories and the lines are parallel. With an interaction, the effect of Predictor 1 is different according to the category of Predictor 2 and the lines are not parallel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-interaction-lines
#| fig-cap: "A sketch of the effect of Predictor 1 on the outcome for the two categories of Predictor 2, without an interaction (left) and with an interaction (right). The lines are drawn for the illustration and do not come from data."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels with a blue and a red rising line, one for each category of Predictor 2. Left, titled No interaction: the two lines are parallel. Right, titled Interaction: the blue line is steep and the red line is almost flat, so the lines fan out."
#| fig-height: 3.2
interaction_sketch <- tribble(
  ~panel,                                ~predictor_2,  ~intercept, ~slope,
  "No interaction: parallel lines",      "category A",  3,          0.5,
  "No interaction: parallel lines",      "category B",  1,          0.5,
  "Interaction: the lines are not parallel", "category A", 2,       0.7,
  "Interaction: the lines are not parallel", "category B", 2,       0.1
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = unique(panel))) |>
  tidyr::crossing(predictor_1 = c(0, 10)) |>
  mutate(outcome = intercept + slope * predictor_1)

ggplot(interaction_sketch, aes(predictor_1, outcome, colour = predictor_2)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("category A" = book_col("blue"), "category B" = book_col("red"))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor 1", y = "Outcome", colour = "Predictor 2") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

### Types of model {#sec-l02-types}

There are three types of model: simple models, mediation models and structural equation models.

#### Simple model

A **simple model** has one or more predictors and only one outcome. It is made of main effects or/and interaction effects. Simple models are the most statistically powerful, easy to test and reliable models. Always prefer a simple model compared to a more complicated solution.

::: {.callout-important title="Warning"}
Including an interaction effect requires a significantly higher sample size.
:::

In the example of @fig-l02-simple, Salary, Gender and Age are the predictors of Job Satisfaction, which is a latent variable and so a circle. Salary and Gender have an interaction effect. This model tests four hypotheses: 3 main effects and 1 interaction effect.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-simple
//| fig-cap: "A simple model with three main effects and one interaction effect."
//| fig-alt: "Three boxes, Salary, Gender and Age, and a circle labelled Job Satisfaction. Age has an arrow to the circle. Salary and the circle are joined by a line with an arrowhead at the circle, and Gender has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.11
//| fig-height: 1.48

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Salary"; "Gender"; "Age"
  node [shape = circle, width = 1, fixedsize = true]
  "Job\nSatisfaction"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Age" -> "Job\nSatisfaction"
  "Gender" -> ""
  "Salary" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> "Job\nSatisfaction"

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Gender"; "";
  }
  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Age"; "Salary";
  }
}
```

#### Mediation model

A **mediation model** (simple or moderated) has at least 2 predictors, one of them being called the **mediator**, and only one outcome. It is made of main effects only for a simple mediation, and of main and interaction effects for a moderated mediation.

A mediation model is a complex path analysis between 3 variables, where one of them explains the relationship between the other two. It is usually used to identify cognitive processes in psychology. @fig-l02-mediation shows an example with Exam Results, Self-Esteem and Happiness. This model tests one hypothesis, 1 mediation effect, but it requires 2 main effects.

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: mediator"}
In a mediation model, the **mediator** is the variable that explains the relationship between the two other variables. In @fig-l02-mediation, Self-Esteem is the mediator: it is predicted by Exam Results and it predicts Happiness.
:::

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-mediation
//| fig-cap: "A mediation model with Exam Results, Self-Esteem and Happiness."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Exam Results with arrows to two ovals, Self-Esteem and Happiness, and an arrow from Self-Esteem to Happiness."
//| fig-width: 4.63
//| fig-height: 0.79

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = box]
  "Exam Results"
  node [shape = oval]
  "Self-Esteem"; Happiness

  "Exam Results" -> {Happiness "Self-Esteem"}
  "Self-Esteem" -> Happiness

}
```

#### Structural equation model {#sec-l02-sem}

A **structural equation model** (SEM) has at least 2 predictors (usually latent variables) and one or more outcomes. It is made of main or/and interaction effects. It is a complex path analysis between multiple variables, including multiple outcomes, and using factor analysis for latent variable estimation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Item contribution to a latent variable"}
The relationship between items of a scale and their corresponding latent variable is considered as significant by default if the scale is valid.
:::

In @fig-l02-sem, each latent variable (oval) is measured by its items (boxes). For example, this model tests four hypotheses.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-sem
//| fig-cap: "A structural equation model: latent variables (ovals) measured by items (boxes), and the arrows between the variables."
//| fig-alt: "Three ovals, Perceived Ease-of-use, Perceived Usefulness and Intention to Use, each linked by plain lines to its own boxes: PEOU1 to PEOU4, PU1 to PU5, and BI1 and BI2. Arrows run from Perceived Ease-of-use to Perceived Usefulness and to Intention to Use, from Perceived Usefulness to Intention to Use, and from Intention to Use to a box labelled Actual Use."
//| fig-width: 5.6
//| fig-height: 5.5

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = oval]
  "Perceived Ease-of-use"; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Intention to Use"

  node [shape = box]
  PU1; PU2; PU3; PU4; PU5; PEOU1; PEOU2; PEOU3; PEOU4; BI1; BI2; "Actual Use"

  {PU1 PU2 PU3 PU4 PU5} -> "Perceived Usefulness" [arrowhead = none]
  {PEOU1 PEOU2 PEOU3 PEOU4} -> "Perceived Ease-of-use" [arrowhead = none]
  {BI1 BI2} -> "Intention to Use" [arrowhead = none]

  "Perceived Usefulness" -> "Intention to Use"
  "Perceived Ease-of-use" -> {"Perceived Usefulness" "Intention to Use"}
  "Intention to Use" -> "Actual Use"

  subgraph {
      rank = same; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Perceived Ease-of-use";
  }

  subgraph {
      rank = same; PU1; PU2; PU3; PU4; PU5; PEOU1; PEOU2; PEOU3; PEOU4; BI1; BI2;
  }

}
```

### What makes a good model {#sec-l02-good}

A good model has the following qualities:

- **Comprehensiveness**: explains a wide range of phenomena.
- **Internal consistency**: propositions and assumptions are consistent and fit together in a coherent manner.
- **Parsimony**: contains only those concepts and assumptions essential for the explanation of a phenomenon.
- **Testability**: concepts and relational statements are precise.
- **Empirical validity**: holds up when tested in the real world.

@fig-l02-good gives an example of a good model: it is the model of @fig-l02-sem without the items of the scales.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-good
//| fig-cap: "An example of a good model, without the items of the scales."
//| fig-alt: "Three ovals and a box. Perceived Ease-of-use has arrows to Perceived Usefulness and to Intention to Use, Perceived Usefulness has an arrow to Intention to Use, and Intention to Use has an arrow to a box labelled Actual Use."
//| fig-width: 5.6
//| fig-height: 1.1

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = oval]
  "Perceived Ease-of-use"; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Intention to Use"

  node [shape = box]
  "Actual Use"

  "Perceived Usefulness" -> "Intention to Use"
  "Perceived Ease-of-use" -> {"Perceived Usefulness" "Intention to Use"}
  "Intention to Use" -> "Actual Use"

  subgraph {
      rank = same; "Perceived Usefulness"; "Perceived Ease-of-use";
  }
}
```

On the contrary, a bad theory or model is too complicated, does not explain many things and cannot be tested.

### Drawing a model {#sec-l02-drawing}

The representation of a model can easily be done directly in a manuscript written with Microsoft Word. For more details, it is also possible to draw the model in Microsoft PowerPoint and to copy-paste it in Microsoft Word.

::: {.callout-important title="Warning"}
- Do NOT fill boxes with any colour, use only black and white.
- Use line arrows, no thick arrows allowed.
:::

Besides MS Word and PowerPoint, there are some ways to draw models in a nicer way.

**Flowchart software and websites.** There are many of them and Google would find them very quickly but, to my knowledge, <https://www.diagrams.net/> is free, easy to use and very efficient.

**Flowchart coding languages.** Going further into the details of how to design academic models, flowchart coding languages are the ultimate step. Instead of using a GUI, it is possible to draw models from a couple of lines of code, which is faster after practising a lot. To my knowledge, the main flowchart coding language tools implementing the [DOT style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)) are: <!-- check: the slide lists mermaid-js, viz-js and nomnoml as DOT style tools; as far as I know only viz-js reads DOT, while mermaid and nomnoml have their own syntax -->

- [mermaid-js](http://mermaid-js.github.io/mermaid/##/) <!-- check: the slide link ends with "##/", probably a typo for "#/" -->
- [viz-js](http://viz-js.com/)
- [nomnoml](https://www.nomnoml.com/)

But [many more alternatives can be used](https://modeling-languages.com/text-uml-tools-complete-list/).

### The DOT language {#sec-l02-dot}

It is easy to start by following these rules:

- Variable names must not include space between words <!-- check: the rule says that names must not include spaces, but the slide examples use quoted names with spaces such as "Predictor 1" -->
- Arrows are represented by the characters `-` and `>`

::: {.callout-warning .box-mistake title="Common mistake: a name with spaces and no quotes"}
A name made of several words, such as Predictor 1, must be written between double quotes, as in all the examples below. Without quotes, DOT reads each word as a separate variable: `Predictor 1 -> Outcome` draws Predictor on its own and an arrow from 1 to Outcome.
:::

What you type:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

What you get is shown in @fig-l02-dot-basic.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-dot-basic
//| fig-cap: "The diagram drawn by the first DOT code."
//| fig-alt: "Two ovals, Predictor 1 and Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing down to an oval labelled Outcome."
//| fig-width: 2.84
//| fig-height: 1.37

digraph {
  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

To modify the orientation and the shape of the box, add the following options:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

The result is shown in @fig-l02-dot-options.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-dot-options
//| fig-cap: "The diagram drawn with the options for the orientation and the shape of the boxes."
//| fig-alt: "Two boxes, Predictor 1 and Predictor 2, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Outcome on the right."
//| fig-width: 2.23
//| fig-height: 1.16

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Predictor 1" -> "Outcome"
  "Predictor 2" -> "Outcome"
}
```

Unfortunately the way to plot an interaction is much trickier. You have to include an invisible box to design the arrow crossing the main arrow:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

The result is shown in @fig-l02-dot-interaction.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-dot-interaction
//| fig-cap: "An interaction effect drawn with an invisible box."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Predictor 1 and a box labelled Outcome joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Outcome. A box labelled Predictor 2 has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.58
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Predictor 1"; "Predictor 2"; "Outcome"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Predictor 2" -> ""
  "Predictor 1" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> Outcome

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Predictor 2"; "";
  }
}
```

There are many more rules to make more complicated models, see for more details <https://graphviz.org/doc/info/lang.html>.

**DotUML extension for Google Docs.** This DOT language can easily be implemented with the DotUML extension in Google Docs. DotUML is developed by a company called BML Solutions but as far as I know it is a free plug-in (at least free of money). See <https://dotuml.com> for more details. After installing the extension, use GraphViz and remove the code corresponding to the default example.

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: draw the model(s) of your paper"}
In the research paper you have selected, **draw the model(s) tested.**

Remember, there is only 1 outcome variable per model and it is not possible to draw two models with the same outcome variable.

Send me your figure by email at damien.dupre@dcu.ie **before the next lecture.**
:::

## Understanding the equation used to test hypotheses {#sec-l02-equations}

### A basic equation {#sec-l02-basic}

```{r}
#| label: l02-perfect-data
df <-
  data.frame(
    Observation = letters[1:11],
    Outcome = 10:0,
    Predictor = 10:0
  )
```

Let's imagine the perfect scenario: **your predictor variable explains perfectly the outcome variable**.

The corresponding equation is: $Outcome = Predictor$. @tbl-l02-perfect gives the data of this scenario and @fig-l02-perfect plots them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l02-perfect
#| tbl-cap: "Data of the perfect scenario."
gt(df) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_row_striping()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-perfect
#| fig-cap: "The perfect scenario: all the observations are on the prediction line."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the outcome against the predictor, both from 0 to 10. The 11 points lie exactly on a straight line rising from the bottom left to the top right."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
df |>
  ggplot(aes(Predictor, Outcome, label = Observation)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,10)) +
  theme_bw()
```

In the equation $Outcome = Predictor$, **three coefficients are hidden** because they are unused:

- the **intercept coefficient** $b_{0}$ (i.e., the value of the Outcome when the Predictor = 0) which is 0 in our case
- the **estimate coefficient** $b_{1}$ (i.e., how much the Outcome increases when the Predictor increases by 1) which is 1 in our case
- the **error coefficient** $e$ (i.e., how far from the prediction line the values of the Outcome are) which is 0 in our case

So in general, the relation between a predictor and an outcome can be written as:

$$Outcome = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Predictor + e$$ {#eq-l02-basic}

which is in our case:

$$Outcome = 0 + 1 * Predictor + 0$$

In real data, the observations are never all on the line. @fig-l02-error puts the perfect scenario next to simulated data in which the outcome is the predictor plus a random error. The red segments are the errors $e$: the distance between each observation and the prediction line.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-error
#| fig-cap: "The perfect scenario (left) and a real scenario with simulated data (right). The red segments are the errors, the distance between each observation and the prediction line."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots of the outcome against the predictor from 0 to 10, each with a blue prediction line. Left, titled Perfect scenario: the 11 points are on the line and there is no error. Right, titled Real scenario: the 11 points are scattered around the line and red vertical segments join each point to the line."
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(34)
real_scenario <- tibble(
  Predictor = 0:10,
  Outcome = Predictor + rnorm(11, mean = 0, sd = 1.2)
)

real_model <- lm(Outcome ~ Predictor, data = real_scenario)
real_scenario <- real_scenario |>
  mutate(predicted = fitted(real_model))

plot_perfect <- ggplot(df, aes(Predictor, Outcome)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-1, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Perfect scenario", subtitle = "b0 = 0, b1 = 1, e = 0 for every observation")

plot_real <- ggplot(real_scenario, aes(Predictor, Outcome)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Predictor, yend = predicted), colour = book_col("red"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(real_model)[[1]], slope = coef(real_model)[[2]], colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-1, 12)) +
  labs(
    title = "Real scenario (simulated data)",
    subtitle = paste0("b0 = ", format_number(coef(real_model)[[1]]), ", b1 = ", format_number(coef(real_model)[[2]]), ", e is not 0")
  )

plot_perfect + plot_real
```

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: error"}
The **error** $e$ is the part of the outcome that the predictors do not explain. For each observation, it is the difference between the actual value of the outcome and the value on the prediction line. It is 0 for every observation only in the perfect scenario.
:::

@eq-l02-basic is the same as the good old $y = ax + b$ (here ordered as $y = b + ax$) where $b_{0}$ is $b$ and $b_{1}$ is $a$. @fig-l02-b0-b1 shows the intercept and the estimate on the prediction line.

<!-- check: in the code below seq(0:10) returns 1 to 11, so the axis breaks start at 1 and not at 0 (seq(0, 10) was probably intended), and the size argument of geom_hline() is deprecated since ggplot2 3.4.0 (linewidth is the current one); the plot is unchanged -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-b0-b1
#| fig-cap: "The intercept b0 and the estimate b1 on the prediction line."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the outcome against the predictor, with 11 points on a rising straight line. A dotted horizontal line at 0 is labelled Intercept b0. A red step of one unit to the right and one unit up, along the line, is labelled Estimate b1."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
data.frame(Predictor = 0:10, Outcome = 0:10) |>
  ggplot(aes(Predictor, Outcome)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", size = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 0.2, label = "Intercept b0") +
  annotate("segment", x = 5, xend = 6, y = 5, yend = 5, color = book_col("red")) +
  annotate("segment", x = 6, xend = 6, y = 5, yend = 6, color = book_col("red")) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.5, y = 5.5, label = "Estimate b1") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0:10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0:10)) +
  theme_bw()
```

In @fig-l02-b0-b1 the line goes through 0 because $b_0 = 0$. @fig-l02-read-line draws a line with another intercept and another estimate, $Outcome = 2 + 0.8\,Predictor$. The intercept is where the line crosses the vertical axis, at $Predictor = 0$. The estimate is how much the line goes up for a step of 1 unit to the right.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-read-line
#| fig-cap: "Reading the intercept and the estimate on the line Outcome = 2 + 0.8 Predictor. The line is drawn for the illustration and does not come from data."
#| fig-alt: "A rising blue line from an outcome of 2 at a predictor of 0 to an outcome of 10 at a predictor of 10. An orange point where the line crosses the vertical axis is labelled b0 = 2, the outcome when the predictor is 0. Between a predictor of 5 and 6, a black step goes 1 unit to the right and 0.8 up to the line, labelled +1 unit of Predictor and b1 = 0.8."
#| fig-height: 3.6
line_intercept <- 2
line_slope <- 0.8
step_from <- 5
step_to <- step_from + 1
outcome_from <- line_intercept + line_slope * step_from
outcome_to <- line_intercept + line_slope * step_to

ggplot() +
  geom_abline(intercept = line_intercept, slope = line_slope, colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = step_from, xend = step_to, y = outcome_from, yend = outcome_from, linewidth = 1, colour = book_col("ink")) +
  annotate("segment", x = step_to, xend = step_to, y = outcome_from, yend = outcome_to, linewidth = 1, colour = book_col("ink")) +
  annotate("text", x = step_from + 0.5, y = outcome_from - 0.9, label = "+1 unit of Predictor", size = 3.6) +
  annotate("text", x = step_to + 0.2, y = (outcome_from + outcome_to) / 2, label = "b[1] == 0.8", parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 3.8) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = line_intercept, colour = book_col("orange"), size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.35, y = line_intercept - 0.2, label = "b[0] == 2", parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.35, y = line_intercept - 1.05, label = "the Outcome when Predictor = 0", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 10), breaks = 0:10, expand = expansion(add = c(0.3, 0.3))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 10.5), breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor", y = "Outcome")
```

It is very important to know that under **EVERY** statistical test, a similar equation is used (t-test, ANOVA, Chi-square are all linear regressions). <!-- check: the Chi-square test is usually described as a log-linear model rather than a linear regression -->

### Relationship between variables {#sec-l02-relationship}

The relationship between a $Predictor$ and an $Outcome$ variable (stated in a main effect hypothesis or in an interaction effect hypothesis) is analysed in terms of: **"How many units of the Outcome variable increases/decreases/changes when the Predictor increases by 1 unit?"**

For example:

> How much Job Satisfaction increases when the Salary increases by €1?

The value of how much of the Outcome variable changes is called the **estimate** (also called the unstandardised estimate). It uses the letter $b$ in equations (e.g., $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, ...). For example:

> If Job Satisfaction increases by 0.1 on a scale from 0 to 5 when the Salary increases by €1, then *b* associated to Salary is 0.1

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: estimate"}
The **estimate** $b$ of a predictor is the number of units by which the outcome changes when the predictor increases by 1 unit. It is positive when the outcome increases, negative when the outcome decreases, and 0 when the outcome stays the same.
:::

@fig-l02-b-signs shows the three cases. The middle one, $b_1 = 0$, is the null hypothesis: the outcome stays the same when the predictor increases.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-b-signs
#| fig-cap: "The sign of the estimate gives the direction of the relationship. The red line is the null hypothesis, b1 = 0. The lines are drawn for the illustration and do not come from data."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels with one line each, the outcome against the predictor. Left, titled b1 above 0, increases: a rising blue line. Middle, titled b1 = 0, stays the same: a flat red line. Right, titled b1 below 0, decreases: a falling blue line."
#| fig-height: 2.8
sign_panels <- c(
  "b1 > 0: increases",
  "b1 = 0: stays the same",
  "b1 < 0: decreases"
)

estimate_signs <- tribble(
  ~panel,         ~intercept, ~slope, ~line_role,
  sign_panels[1], 2,          0.6,    "model",
  sign_panels[2], 5,          0,      "null",
  sign_panels[3], 8,          -0.6,   "model"
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = sign_panels)) |>
  tidyr::crossing(predictor = c(0, 10)) |>
  mutate(outcome = intercept + slope * predictor)

ggplot(estimate_signs, aes(predictor, outcome, colour = line_role)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("model" = book_col("blue"), "null" = book_col("red")), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor", y = "Outcome") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank())
```

To evaluate if the strength of the relationship $b$ between a predictor and an outcome variable is significant, an equation is statistically tested using all the predictors related to the same outcome. The basic equation of a statistical model is:

$$Outcome = b_0 + b_n \,Predictors + Error$$

where the $Predictors$ includes all the $n$ variables used as predictor in formulated hypotheses using this specific $Outcome$ variable and being associated to a specific $b$ estimate. This expresses the idea that the outcome can be described by one or multiple predictors, and that the remaining part of the outcome's variability that is not explained by the predictors is called the error.

### Equations, variables and effect types {#sec-l02-effect-types}

Except in special cases:

- an outcome (or dependent variable) has to be continuous
- a predictor can be continuous or categorical

For example:

$$Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Origin + e$$

In this equation, $Salary$ is continuous with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{1}$) and $Origin$ is categorical with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{2}$).

An interaction effect is represented by multiplying the 2 predictors involved:

$$Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Origin + b_{3}\,Salary*Origin + e$$

In this equation, $Salary$ is continuous with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{1}$), $Origin$ is categorical with a main effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{2}$), and $Salary$ with $Origin$ have an interaction effect on $Job\,Satisfaction$ ($b_{3}$).

@fig-l02-terms puts the model of this equation next to its terms. Each arrow of the model is one term of the equation, and each estimate $b$ tests one hypothesis. The intercept $b_{0}$ and the error $e$ have no arrow, because they do not test a hypothesis.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-terms
#| fig-cap: "Each arrow of the model is one term of the equation, and each estimate b tests one hypothesis."
#| fig-alt: "On the left, a model in black and white: three boxes, Salary, Origin and Salary * Origin, with arrows labelled b1, b2 and b3 to a box Job Satisfaction. On the right, one row per arrow gives the term of the equation and the hypothesis it tests: b1 Salary, the main effect of Salary; b2 Origin, the main effect of Origin; b3 Salary * Origin, the interaction effect of Salary and Origin. Under them, the full equation."
#| fig-height: 3.2
model_boxes <- tribble(
  ~label,             ~x,  ~y,  ~width,
  "Salary",           1.0, 3.0, 1.7,
  "Origin",           1.0, 2.0, 1.7,
  "Salary * Origin",  1.0, 1.0, 1.7,
  "Job\nSatisfaction", 4.0, 2.0, 1.4
)

model_arrows <- tribble(
  ~y_from, ~y_to, ~estimate, ~term,                 ~hypothesis,
  3.0,     2.2,   "b[1]",    "b[1]~Salary",          "main effect of Salary",
  2.0,     2.0,   "b[2]",    "b[2]~Origin",          "main effect of Origin",
  1.0,     1.8,   "b[3]",    "b[3]~Salary*'*'*Origin", "interaction effect of\nSalary and Origin"
)

column_titles <- tribble(
  ~x,  ~label,
  2.5, "Model",
  6.1, "Term of the equation",
  8.6, "Hypothesis tested"
)

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = model_boxes, aes(x, y, width = width), height = 0.62, fill = "white", colour = book_col("ink"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = model_boxes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(
    data = model_arrows,
    aes(x = 1.85, xend = 3.3, y = y_from, yend = y_to),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.16, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    colour = book_col("ink"), linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_text(data = model_arrows, aes(x = 2.25, y = y_from + (y_to - y_from) * 0.28 + 0.24, label = estimate), parse = TRUE, size = 3.8) +
  geom_text(data = model_arrows, aes(x = 5.3, y = y_from, label = term), parse = TRUE, hjust = 0, size = 3.8) +
  geom_text(data = model_arrows, aes(x = 7.9, y = y_from, label = hypothesis), hjust = 0, size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = column_titles, aes(x, y = 3.75, label = label), fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 5.6, y = 0.15, size = 3.8, parse = TRUE,
    label = "Job~Satisfaction == b[0] + b[1]~Salary + b[2]~Origin + b[3]~Salary*'*'*Origin + e"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 10.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.1, 3.95)) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the equation of the simple model"}
The simple model of @fig-l02-simple has four arrows: the main effects of Salary, Gender and Age, and the interaction effect of Salary and Gender. Its equation has one estimate per arrow: $Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Gender + b_{3}\,Age + b_{4}\,Salary*Gender + e$. The four estimates $b_{1}$ to $b_{4}$ test the four hypotheses.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .box-mistake title="Common mistake: an interaction without its main effects"}
An equation such as $Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{3}\,Salary*Origin + e$ is incomplete. An interaction effect involves the main effect of each predictor involved, so the equation must also contain $b_{1}\,Salary$ and $b_{2}\,Origin$, and the hypotheses must include the two main effect hypotheses.
:::

### The relevance of the intercept {#sec-l02-intercept}

To test hypotheses, only the $b$ values associated to predictors (independent variables) are important. The intercept is always included in an equation but its result is useless for hypothesis testing. Let's see why the intercept is always included but discarded most of the time.

Imagine we want to test the relationship between GDP per Capita and Life Expectancy of countries in the world. Let's compare a model without and a model with intercept:

- Without intercept: $Life\,Expectancy = b_{1}\,GDP\,per\,Capita + e$
- With intercept: $Life\,Expectancy = b_{0} + b_{1}\,GDP\,per\,Capita + e$

@fig-l02-intercept shows the original data (A), the model without intercept (B) and the model with intercept (C). If the intercept is not included, the intercept is zero and can lead to estimation errors.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-intercept
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy and GDP per capita of the countries of the world in 2007 (gapminder data): the original data (A), the model without intercept (B) and the model with intercept (C)."
#| fig-alt: "Three scatter plots of life expectancy against GDP per capita. Panel A shows the original data only. Panel B adds a fitted line forced through the origin. Panel C adds a fitted line with an intercept."
#| fig-height: 5.5
p1 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(
    title = "A: Original Data",
    x = "GDP per Capita ($)",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  )

p2 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE, formula = "y ~ x + 0 ") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(
    title = "B: Model without intercept",
    x = "GDP per Capita ($)",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  )

p3 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE, formula = "y ~ x") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 90)) +
  labs(
    title = "C: Model with intercept",
    x = "GDP per Capita ($)",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  )

p1 / (p2 + p3)
```

```{r}
#| label: l02-intercept-models
#| include: false
countries_2007 <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007)

model_without_intercept <- lm(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap + 0, data = countries_2007)
model_with_intercept <- lm(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap, data = countries_2007)

b1_without <- coef(model_without_intercept)[["gdpPercap"]]
b0_with <- coef(model_with_intercept)[["(Intercept)"]]
b1_with <- coef(model_with_intercept)[["gdpPercap"]]
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the estimate of GDP per capita with and without the intercept"}
Without the intercept, $b_{1} = `r format_number(b1_without, 5)`$: life expectancy increases by `r format_number(b1_without * 1000)` years when GDP per capita increases by 1,000 dollars. With the intercept, $b_{0} = `r format_number(b0_with)`$ and $b_{1} = `r format_number(b1_with, 5)`$, that is `r format_number(b1_with * 1000)` years for 1,000 dollars. Leaving out the intercept multiplies the estimate by `r format_number(b1_without / b1_with, 1)`.
:::

@fig-l02-intercept-errors shows where this estimation error comes from. Without the intercept, the line has to pass through 0 (a life expectancy of 0 for a GDP per capita of 0), so it is far below the poorest countries and far above the richest ones: the errors are large and they depend on GDP per capita. With the intercept, the errors are smaller and spread around 0.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-intercept-errors
#| fig-cap: "The errors of the model without intercept (B) and of the model with intercept (C), for the countries of the world in 2007 (gapminder data)."
#| fig-alt: "Two scatter plots of the error, in years of life expectancy, against GDP per capita, with a grey horizontal line at 0. Left, B, model without intercept: the red points are far above 0 for the poorest countries, up to about 67 years, and far below 0 for the richest ones, down to about -65 years. Right, C, model with intercept: the red points stay between about -23 and 13 years around 0."
#| fig-height: 3.4
intercept_errors <- bind_rows(
  countries_2007 |>
    mutate(model = "B: Model without intercept", error = residuals(model_without_intercept)),
  countries_2007 |>
    mutate(model = "C: Model with intercept", error = residuals(model_with_intercept))
)

ggplot(intercept_errors, aes(gdpPercap, error)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = book_col("grey"), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = book_col("red"), size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), breaks = c(0, 20000, 40000)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per Capita ($)", y = "Error (years)")
```

::: {.callout-warning .box-mistake title="Common mistake: removing the intercept because no hypothesis is about it"}
The intercept does not test a hypothesis, but it is not optional. Without it, the line is forced through 0 and the estimates of the predictors can be wrong, as for GDP per capita above. Keep $b_{0}$ in every equation and test the hypotheses with the estimates of the predictors.
:::

### Notes on the notation of equations {#sec-l02-notation}

Equations are not always written in the same way. Here are four notes on the notation.

1. **Greek or Latin alphabet?**

   $$Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,X_{1} + \epsilon \; vs. \; Y = b_{0} + b_{1}\,X_{1} + e$$

2. **Subscript $i$ or not?**

   $$Y = b_{0} + b_{1}\,X_{1} + e \; vs. \; Y_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1}\,X_{1_{i}} + e_{i}$$

3. **Which sign between estimates and predictors?**

   $$Y = b_{0} + b_{1}.X_{1} + b_{2}*X_{2} + b_{3}\,X_{3} + e$$

4. **Hat on $Y$ or not? Capital letter or not?**

   $$\hat{Y}\; or\; \hat{y}\; vs.\; Y\; or\; y$$

### Representing an equation {#sec-l02-repr-eq}

Exactly like with models, there are different ways to communicate an equation in academic research outputs.

The least sophisticated approach would be to type the equation in Microsoft Word and to apply some italics and subscript style a posteriori. While there is nothing wrong with this approach, note that Microsoft Word has a tool to insert equations (Insert > Equations), then a GUI will help you to design special characters in equations.

Now there is a better way, which is also more complicated. LaTeX is used for entire manuscripts with all the specific design requirements imposed by the style of academic journals. LaTeX is hell and we will see a specific approach to avoid it, but the LaTeX style for equations is the best. <!-- check: "we will see a specific approach to avoid it" refers to a later lecture that the slide does not name -->

::: {.callout-tip .box-howto title="In LaTeX: an equation"}
Here are the most basic rules:

- Start with `\begin{equation}` and end with `\end{equation}`
- Space between words can be added with `\,`
- To subscript a number use the underscore sign `_`

For example:

```{.latex}
\begin{equation}
  Outcome = b_0 + b_1\,Predictor 1 + b_2\,Predictor 2 + e
\end{equation}
```

Is translated as:

$$Outcome = b_0 + b_1\,Predictor 1 + b_2\,Predictor 2 +e$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip .box-howto title="In Google Docs: an equation with Auto-LaTeX Equations"}
**Auto-LaTeX Equations for Google Docs.** Another fantastic extension is available for Google Docs, called Auto-LaTeX Equations. Instead of using `\begin{equation}` and `\end{equation}`, use `$$` to open and close the equation. Then, click on "Render Equation", for the equation to be transformed in LaTeX style. Note that some websites can help to create the LaTeX code, see for example <https://latex.codecogs.com/eqneditor/editor.php>.
:::

**quiver.** quiver is a modern, graphical editor for commutative and pasting diagrams, capable of rendering high-quality diagrams for screen viewing, and exporting to LaTeX via tikz-cd or Typst via fletcher. See <https://q.uiver.app/>.

### Practice: from results to model and equation {#sec-l02-practice}

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: from results to model and equation"}
I will show you some results. Using these results:

1. Identify the role of variables,
2. Formulate the tested hypotheses,
3. Draw the corresponding model, and
4. Translate it in an equation.

Two examples follow, each with its solution.
:::

```{r}
#| label: l02-ex1-data
df3 <- tibble(
  Participant = c("ppt1", "ppt2", "ppt3", "ppt4", "ppt5", "ppt6"),
  `Sleep Time` = c(9, 5, 8.5, 7, 6.5, 5.5),
  `Exam Results` = c(89, 64, 71, 77, 78, 69)
)
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: Example 1"}
Using the results obtained, identify the role of variables, formulate the tested hypotheses, draw the corresponding model, and translate it in an equation. @tbl-l02-ex1 gives the data and @fig-l02-ex1 the visualisation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l02-ex1
#| tbl-cap: "Data of Example 1."
df3 |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-ex1
#| fig-cap: "Exam results according to sleep time for the six participants of Example 1."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of exam results against sleep time. Each of the six points is labelled with its participant, ppt1 to ppt6."
#| fig-height: 3.5
df3 |>
  ggplot(aes(`Sleep Time`, `Exam Results`, label = Participant)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  geom_text_repel() +
  theme_bw()
```

Suggested time: 5 minutes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution title="Solution" collapse="true"}
**Variables**

- Outcome = Exam Results (from 0 to 100)
- Predictor = Sleep Time (from 0 to Inf.)

**Alternative hypothesis**

- $H_a$: **Exam Results** *increase* when **Sleep Time** increases
- ($H_0$: **Exam Results** *stay the same* when **Sleep Time** increases)

**Model** (@fig-l02-ex1-model)

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-ex1-model
//| fig-cap: "The model of Example 1."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Sleep Time with an arrow labelled b1 pointing to a box labelled Exam Results."
//| fig-width: 2.73
//| fig-height: 0.52

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]

  "Sleep Time" -> "Exam Results" [label= b1]
}
```

**Equation**

$$Exam\,Results = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Sleep\,Time + e$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: l02-ex1-estimates
#| include: false
model_example_1 <- lm(`Exam Results` ~ `Sleep Time`, data = df3)
example_1_b0 <- coef(model_example_1)[[1]]
example_1_b1 <- coef(model_example_1)[[2]]
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the estimates of Example 1"}
With the six participants of Example 1, the equation is estimated as $Exam\,Results = `r format_number(example_1_b0)` + `r format_number(example_1_b1)`\,Sleep\,Time + e$. The estimate $b_{1} = `r format_number(example_1_b1)`$ means that the exam results increase by `r format_number(example_1_b1)` points when sleep time increases by 1 hour. @sec-lecture-04 shows how to obtain these values and how to test them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: l02-ex2-data
df4 <- tibble(
  Participant = c("ppt1", "ppt2", "ppt3", "ppt4", "ppt5", "ppt6"),
  `Sleep Time` = c(9, 5, 8.5, 7, 6.5, 5.5),
  Age = c(50, 60, 70, 20, 30, 40),
  `Exam Results` = c(89, 64, 71, 77, 52, 69),
  Age_c = c("experienced", "experienced", "experienced", "beginner", "beginner", "beginner")
)
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: Example 2"}
Using the results obtained, identify the role of variables, formulate the tested hypotheses, draw the corresponding model, and translate it in an equation. @tbl-l02-ex2 gives the data and @fig-l02-ex2 the visualisation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l02-ex2
#| tbl-cap: "Data of Example 2."
df4 |>
  select(-Age) |>
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l02-ex2
#| fig-cap: "Exam results according to sleep time for the six participants of Example 2, by age category."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of exam results against sleep time with one straight line for each age category, beginner and experienced, drawn in two colours."
#| fig-height: 3.2
df4 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `Sleep Time`, y = `Exam Results`, color = Age_c)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Suggested time: 5 minutes.
:::

::::: {.callout-note .box-solution title="Solution" collapse="true"}
**Variables**

- Outcome = Exam Results (from 0 to 100)
- Predictor 1 = Sleep Time (from 0 to Inf.)
- Predictor 2 = Age (experienced vs beginner)

**Alternative hypotheses**

- $H_{a_{1}}$: **Exam Results** *increase* when **Sleep Time** increases
- $H_{a_{2}}$: **Exam Results** of **experienced students** are *higher* than for **beginner students**
- $H_{a_{3}}$: The effect of **Sleep Time** on **Exam Results** is *higher* for **experienced** than for **beginner students**

**Model** (@fig-l02-ex2-model)

::: {#fig-l02-ex2-model}

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-ex2-model-classic
//| fig-cap: "Classic representation."
//| fig-alt: "A box labelled Sleep Time and a box labelled Exam Results joined by a horizontal line with an arrowhead at Exam Results. A box labelled Age has an arrow pointing down to the middle of that line."
//| fig-width: 3.63
//| fig-height: 0.94

digraph {
 graph [rankdir = LR]

 node [shape = box]
 "Sleep Time"; "Exam Results"; Age
 node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
 ""

 Age -> ""
 "Sleep Time" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
 ""-> "Exam Results"

 subgraph {
   rank = same; Age; "";
 }
}
```

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l02-ex2-model-effects
//| fig-cap: "Effects correspondence."
//| fig-alt: "Three boxes, Sleep Time, Age and Sleep Time * Age, each with an arrow pointing to a box labelled Exam Results. The arrows are labelled b1, b2 and b3 respectively."
//| fig-width: 3.17
//| fig-height: 1.79

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]

  node [shape = box]
  "Sleep Time"; "Exam Results"; Age; "Sleep Time * Age"

  Age -> "Exam Results" [label= b2]
  "Sleep Time" -> "Exam Results" [label= b1]
  "Sleep Time * Age" -> "Exam Results" [label= b3]

  }
```

The model of Example 2.
:::

**Equation**

$$Exam\,Results = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Sleep\,Time + b_{2}\,Age + b_{3}\,Sleep\,Time*Age + e$$
:::::

## Conclusion {#sec-l02-conclusion}

To summarise, follow these steps:

1. **Variables**
    - Identify the role and type of each of your variables.
2. **Hypotheses**
    - Formulate your alternative hypotheses by using the proposed templates (@sec-lecture-01).
    - Any other formulation, even if it makes sense, is not good practice (for example using the terms "has an impact", "is related to", "influences", ...).
    - An interaction hypothesis requires the formulation of the main effect hypothesis of each predictor involved.
3. **Model**
    - A model should represent all your hypotheses and only your hypotheses.
    - Draw only one model per outcome variable (except when doing SEM analyses).
    - Use the same names or acronyms as your hypotheses.
4. **Equation**
    - Formulate your equation(s) in every paper that you want to submit (if reviewers want to remove it, they will tell you).

::: {.callout-note .box-keypoints title="Key points"}
- A model gives an overview of the predicted relationships between variables. Every arrow is a tested hypothesis, every tested hypothesis is an arrow, and each model has only one outcome variable (except SEM models).
- A simple arrow is a main effect and a crossing arrow is an interaction effect. Squares are measured items and circles are latent variables.
- Prefer a simple model: it is more powerful, easier to test and more reliable. Including an interaction effect requires a larger sample size.
- Draw models in black and white with line arrows, using Word, PowerPoint, flowchart software or DOT code.
- Under every statistical test a similar equation is used, $Outcome = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Predictor + e$, where $b_{0}$ is the intercept, $b_{1}$ is the estimate (the change of the outcome when the predictor increases by 1) and $e$ is the error.
- The intercept is always included in the equation, but the hypotheses are tested with the estimates of the predictors. Leaving the intercept out forces it to zero and can lead to estimation errors.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-l02-exercises}

These exercises practise the steps of the chapter: from hypotheses to a model, from a model to an equation, and the code to write them. The first ones need only a pen. For the DOT and LaTeX exercises, use an editor such as <http://viz-js.com/> or <https://latex.codecogs.com/eqneditor/editor.php> to check your code.

::: {#exr-l02-vocabulary}
## True or false?

Say whether each statement is true or false, and correct the false ones.

a. Every arrow of a model corresponds to a hypothesis to be tested.
b. A simple model can include two outcome variables if they are measured on the same participants.
c. A latent variable, such as job satisfaction measured with several questions, is drawn as a square.
d. A model with two predictors and their interaction effect tests three hypotheses.
e. In $Outcome = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Predictor + e$, $b_{0}$ is how much the outcome increases when the predictor increases by 1.
f. The hypotheses are tested with the estimates of the predictors, not with the intercept.
g. In an equation, an interaction effect is written by adding the two predictors involved.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
a. True. This is Rule 1, and Rule 2 says the reverse: every tested hypothesis has an arrow.
b. False. Each model has only one outcome variable (Rule 4). Only a structural equation model can have several outcomes.
c. False. A latent variable is drawn as a circle (or an oval). Squares are actual measures or items.
d. True. It tests the main effect of each predictor and the interaction effect: 2 main effects and 1 interaction effect.
e. False. $b_{0}$ is the intercept, the value of the outcome when the predictor is 0. How much the outcome increases when the predictor increases by 1 is the estimate $b_{1}$.
f. True. The intercept is always included in the equation, but it does not test a hypothesis.
g. False. An interaction effect is written by multiplying the two predictors, for example $b_{3}\,Salary*Origin$.
:::

::: {#exr-l02-count}
## Counting the hypotheses of a model

Look at the three models of @fig-l02-count.

1. How many hypotheses does each model test? Say which ones are main effects and which ones are interaction effects.
2. In each model, which variables are latent variables?
3. How many estimates $b$, without counting the intercept $b_{0}$, will the equation of each model have?
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. Model A tests 2 hypotheses: the main effects of Salary and of Age. Model B tests 3 hypotheses: the main effects of Sleep Time and of Breakfast, and their interaction effect (the crossing arrow involves the main effects of both predictors). Model C tests 5 hypotheses: the main effects of Salary, Gender, Age and Location, and the interaction effect of Salary and Gender.
2. Job Satisfaction in Model A and Work Motivation in Model C, because they are drawn as circles. All the other variables are measures (squares).
3. One estimate per hypothesis: 2 in Model A, 3 in Model B and 5 in Model C.
:::

::: {#exr-l02-draw}
## From hypotheses to a model

The manager of a company formulates three hypotheses. Work motivation is measured with a scale of five questions, salary is measured in euro, and gender has two categories (female and male).

- $H_{a_{1}}$: **Work motivation** *increases* when **salary** increases
- $H_{a_{2}}$: The **work motivation** of **female employees** is *higher* than the **work motivation** of **male employees**
- $H_{a_{3}}$: The effect of **salary** on **work motivation** is *higher* for **female employees** than it is for **male employees**

1. Identify the role and the type of each variable.
2. Draw the model, with the right shapes and the right arrows.
3. Draw the same model with the interaction as a predictor of its own, and write on each arrow the estimate $b$ that tests it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. Outcome: Work Motivation, continuous and latent (five questions), so a circle. Predictor 1: Salary, continuous and measured, so a square. Predictor 2: Gender, categorical (female vs male) and measured, so a square.
2. $H_{a_{1}}$ and $H_{a_{2}}$ are main effects and $H_{a_{3}}$ is an interaction effect, drawn with a crossing arrow from Gender to the arrow of Salary:

```{dot}
//| label: solution-draw-crossing-arrow
//| fig-width: 3.4
//| fig-height: 1.1

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Salary"; "Gender"
  node [shape = circle, width = 1.15, fixedsize = true]
  "Work\nMotivation"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Gender" -> ""
  "Salary" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> "Work\nMotivation"

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Gender"; "";
  }
}
```

3. With the interaction as a predictor of its own, there are three arrows, one per hypothesis:

```{dot}
//| label: solution-draw-three-arrows
//| fig-width: 3.4
//| fig-height: 1.8

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Salary"; "Gender"; "Salary * Gender"
  node [shape = circle, width = 1.15, fixedsize = true]
  "Work\nMotivation"

  "Salary" -> "Work\nMotivation" [label = b1]
  "Gender" -> "Work\nMotivation" [label = b2]
  "Salary * Gender" -> "Work\nMotivation" [label = b3]
}
```
:::

::: {#exr-l02-equation}
## From a model to an equation

1. Write the equation of the model of @exr-l02-draw.
2. Write the equations of Models A, B and C of @fig-l02-count.
3. Write the equation of question 1 again with the Greek alphabet and the subscript $i$ (@sec-l02-notation).
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. One term per arrow, plus the intercept and the error:
   $$Work\,Motivation = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Gender + b_{3}\,Salary*Gender + e$$
2. Model A: $Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Age + e$

   Model B: $Exam\,Results = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Sleep\,Time + b_{2}\,Breakfast + b_{3}\,Sleep\,Time*Breakfast + e$

   Model C: $Work\,Motivation = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Gender + b_{3}\,Age + b_{4}\,Location + b_{5}\,Salary*Gender + e$

   The order of the terms does not matter, but the main effects usually come before the interaction effects.
3. $b$ becomes $\beta$, $e$ becomes $\epsilon$, and the subscript $i$ (one value per observation) goes on the outcome, on the predictors and on the error:
   $$Work\,Motivation_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\,Salary_{i} + \beta_{2}\,Gender_{i} + \beta_{3}\,Salary_{i}*Gender_{i} + \epsilon_{i}$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: l02-exercise-by-hand
#| include: false
# The exercise done by hand uses the estimates of Example 1 rounded to one decimal, as a reader does.
b0_rounded <- round(example_1_b0, 1)
b1_rounded <- round(example_1_b1, 1)

participant_4 <- df3 |>
  filter(Participant == "ppt4")

predicted_participant_4 <- b0_rounded + b1_rounded * participant_4$`Sleep Time`
error_participant_4 <- participant_4$`Exam Results` - predicted_participant_4
```

::: {#exr-l02-by-hand}
## Intercept, estimate and error by hand

With the six participants of Example 1, the estimated equation, with its values rounded to one decimal, is $Exam\,Results = `r format_number(b0_rounded, 1)` + `r format_number(b1_rounded, 1)`\,Sleep\,Time + e$.

1. By how much do the exam results change when sleep time increases by 1 hour? And by 2 hours?
2. What exam result does the line predict for a sleep time of `r participant_4$"Sleep Time"` hours?
3. Participant `r participant_4$Participant` slept `r participant_4$"Sleep Time"` hours and obtained `r participant_4$"Exam Results"`. What is the error $e$ of this participant? Is the participant above or below the prediction line?
4. What does $b_{0}$ mean here, and why is it not used to test the hypothesis?
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. The estimate is the change for 1 unit: `r format_number(b1_rounded, 1)` points for 1 hour, and $2 \times `r format_number(b1_rounded, 1)` = `r format_number(2 * b1_rounded, 1)`$ points for 2 hours.
2. Replace $Sleep\,Time$ by its value: $`r format_number(b0_rounded, 1)` + `r format_number(b1_rounded, 1)` \times `r participant_4$"Sleep Time"` = `r format_number(predicted_participant_4, 1)`$.
3. The error is the actual value minus the value on the line: $e = `r participant_4$"Exam Results"` - `r format_number(predicted_participant_4, 1)` = `r format_number(error_participant_4, 1)`$. The error is positive, so the participant is above the line: a little better than the model predicts.
4. $b_{0} = `r format_number(b0_rounded, 1)`$ is the exam result predicted for a sleep time of 0 hours. No participant sleeps 0 hours, and the hypothesis is about the effect of sleep time, which is tested with $b_{1}$. The intercept stays in the equation so that $b_{1}$ is estimated correctly.
:::

::: {#exr-l02-dot}
## A model in the DOT language

1. Write the DOT code of the model of @exr-l02-draw (question 2), with the crossing arrow, and check it in a DOT editor such as <http://viz-js.com/>.
2. A classmate writes `Salary -> Work Motivation` without quotes. What does DOT draw?
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. Start from the DOT code of an interaction in @sec-l02-dot, replace the names, and give the outcome the shape of a circle because it is a latent variable:

```{.dot}
digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Salary"; "Gender"
  node [shape = circle, width = 1.15, fixedsize = true]
  "Work\nMotivation"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Gender" -> ""
  "Salary" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> "Work\nMotivation"

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Gender"; "";
  }
}
```

The `\n` breaks the name on two lines so that it fits in the circle. The code draws the model of the solution of @exr-l02-draw.

2. Without quotes, DOT reads each word as a separate variable. It draws an arrow from Salary to Work, and Motivation on its own. The name must be written `"Work Motivation"`.
:::

::: {#exr-l02-latex}
## An equation in LaTeX

Write the LaTeX code of the equation of the model of @exr-l02-draw, following the rules of @sec-l02-repr-eq, and check it in a LaTeX equation editor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Use `\,` for the space between the two words of the outcome and between each estimate and its predictor, and `_` for the subscripts:

```{.latex}
\begin{equation}
  Work\,Motivation = b_0 + b_1\,Salary + b_2\,Gender + b_3\,Salary*Gender + e
\end{equation}
```

It is translated as:

$$Work\,Motivation = b_0 + b_1\,Salary + b_2\,Gender + b_3\,Salary*Gender + e$$
:::

::: {#exr-l02-mistakes}
## Find the mistakes

A student tests three hypotheses. Job satisfaction is measured with four questions.

- $H_{a_{1}}$: **Job satisfaction** *increases* when **salary** increases
- $H_{a_{2}}$: The **job satisfaction** of **Irish employees** is *higher* than the **job satisfaction** of **French employees**
- $H_{a_{3}}$: The effect of **salary** on **job satisfaction** is *higher* for **Irish employees** than it is for **French employees**

The student draws the model of @fig-l02-mistakes-model, fills the boxes in light blue to make the figure nicer, and writes the equation $Job\,Satisfaction = b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Salary*Origin + e$. Find at least five mistakes in the model and in the equation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the model:

- **The arrow from Age has no hypothesis.** Every arrow must correspond to a tested hypothesis (Rule 1). Remove it, or add the hypothesis about age.
- **The model has two outcome variables.** Job Satisfaction and Turnover Intention cannot be the outcomes of the same simple model (Rule 4). Turnover Intention needs its own model and its own hypotheses.
- **Job Satisfaction is drawn as a square.** It is measured with four questions, so it is a latent variable and is drawn as a circle.
- **The boxes are filled with a colour.** Models are drawn in black and white only, with line arrows.

In the equation:

- **The intercept $b_{0}$ is missing.** It is always included, even though it does not test a hypothesis.
- **The main effect of Origin is missing.** An interaction involves the main effect of each predictor, and $H_{a_{2}}$ is tested by the estimate of Origin.

The corrected model and equation:

```{dot}
//| label: solution-mistakes-corrected
//| fig-width: 3.4
//| fig-height: 1.1

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = box]
  "Salary"; "Origin"
  node [shape = circle, width = 1.15, fixedsize = true]
  "Job\nSatisfaction"
  node [shape = point, width = 0, height = 0]
  ""

  "Origin" -> ""
  "Salary" -> "" [arrowhead = none]
  "" -> "Job\nSatisfaction"

  subgraph {
    rank = same; "Origin"; "";
  }
}
```

$$Job\,Satisfaction = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Salary + b_{2}\,Origin + b_{3}\,Salary*Origin + e$$
:::
